title: About a Boy
full_review:
An odd 12-year-old boy helps a shallow, immature man learn about the important things in life in the offbeat comedy-drama "About A Boy" (Universal).

Based on the 1998 best-selling novel by British author Nick Hornby, "About A Boy" was directed by an unlikely choice, Paul and Chris Weitz, better known for their 1999 gross-out comedy "American Pie." But the Weitz brothers combine humor and pathos in a film that pulls on the heartstrings without pouring on the syrup. "About A Boy" never gets too deeply involved in the characters, keeping things mostly light and frothy. But it has enough of a bite to maintain interest in what will happen next with this eclectic, endearing crew. And between fans of Hugh Grant, who plays the lead, and those of author Hornby (whose other best-selling novel, "High Fidelity," was turned into a film starring John Cusack in 2000), the film is likely to attract an audience willing to overlook some of its faults.

The film does have drawbacks, mainly due to its split personality. It can't settle on whether it wants to be a romantic movie or one about a man's journey into self-discovery. But the directors Weitz manage to blend these styles well enough to make the film a diverting time-passer. The jokes aren't the laugh-out-loud type, but they are amusing enough to keep a smile on your face. And when Grant finds his groove as the bumbling romantic lead, his charm shines forth in a nearly irresistible form.

Grant stars as Will, a Peter-Pan type who fears commitment and thoroughly enjoys his child-free, slacker lifestyle. Living off the royalties from his father's corny Christmas song, "Santa Super Sled," Will loafs about free of the responsibilities of a job or career, with only women on his mind. His quest for no-strings-attached relationships leads him to date single moms, whom he views as willing partners too wrapped up in themselves to want more than some carefree dating.

This leads him to join a meeting of SPAT -- Single Parents, Alone Together -- where he's surprised to find that the women are either ugly, men-bashers or a little off-kilter. But he does salvage something by scamming a date with the sole beauty of the group, Suzie (Victoria Smurfit), after inventing a 2-year-old son named Ned to drum up some sympathy and legitimize why he's there in the first place.

Paralleling Will's story is that of grammar-school geek Marcus (Nicholas Hoult), whose mother, Fiona (Toni Collette), still walks him to school, saying "I love you," as they part, much to Marcus' embarrassment and fueling the already mean-spirited bullying he takes at school. An ex-hippie vegetarian who refuses to allow Marcus to go to McDonald's, Fiona doesn't seem to be aware of the tough time her son is going through. The fact that she weeps uncontrollably also points to her emotional imbalance.

Suzie is her supportive best friend, who, on a date with Will, takes Marcus along for the day to give Fiona a break. Here the film's two plots connect, setting the stage for the main story: a rather mature but lonely 12-year-old and an immature but lonely 38-year-old discovering together that everybody needs somebody.

With his Mr. Spock eyebrows and page-boy haircut, Hoult is convincing as a bullied boy yearning for a manly role model or even just a friend to help him forget about his problems at home and at school. Will is appropriately cool to the young boy, unable to figure out just what Marcus may want from a self-absorbed cad such as himself. The warming up to each other, though inevitable, grows naturally. Some of the best scenes are of the two of them just sitting around in Will's fab bachelor pad, watching the British quiz show "Countdown" without really saying as much as a word to each other.

"About A Boy" is really about two boys, one thrust into the adult world of handling an unstable mother and the pressures of pre-teendom, and the other trying to stave off the responsibilities of adulthood despite already being an adult. The film doesn't tap the emotional depths it could have, considering the source material, but it is nonetheless entertaining fare for the adult moviegoer.

Due to an attempted suicide, a few sexual references, much profanity and fleeting rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
